items.q: Entry of the pollen tube into the ovule through the chalaza instead of the micropyle is called
items.why: When the pollen tube enters the ovule through the base (chalaza) instead of the micropyle, the phenomenon is called chalazogamy, seen in Casuarina.

items.q: The hormone mainly responsible for maintaining pregnancy by preventing uterine contractions is
items.why: Progesterone, secreted by the corpus luteum and later the placenta, maintains the endometrium and suppresses uterine contractions throughout pregnancy.

items.q: A test cross between a heterozygous tall pea plant (Tt) and a homozygous dwarf plant (tt) gives offspring in the ratio
items.why: Tt x tt gives Tt and tt offspring in equal proportion, i.e. a 1:1 ratio, confirming the genotype of the tall parent as heterozygous.

items.q: The enzyme that joins Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand during DNA replication is
items.why: DNA ligase seals the nicks between adjacent Okazaki fragments on the discontinuously synthesized lagging strand.

items.q: Which of the following does NOT disturb Hardy-Weinberg genetic equilibrium in a population?
items.why: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium assumes random mating among individuals; it is the other factors (mutation, drift, selection, migration) that change allele frequencies and disturb equilibrium.

items.q: Loss of water in liquid droplet form from the margins of leaves, typically at night, is called
items.why: Guttation is the exudation of water droplets from specialized pores (hydathodes) on leaf margins, usually under conditions of high root pressure and humidity.

items.q: Which plant growth regulator is a gas and promotes fruit ripening and abscission?
items.why: Ethylene is a gaseous hormone that hastens fruit ripening, promotes senescence and abscission of leaves and flowers.

items.q: The pacemaker of the human heart, which initiates the heartbeat, is the
items.why: The sino-atrial (SA) node, located in the wall of the right atrium, generates rhythmic electrical impulses that initiate each heartbeat, hence it is called the natural pacemaker.

items.q: Haemoglobin has the highest affinity for which of the following gases, making it dangerous in poisoning?
items.why: Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin about 200 times more strongly than oxygen, forming stable carboxyhaemoglobin and blocking oxygen transport.

items.q: Which part of the human brain controls involuntary vital functions like heartbeat, breathing and blood pressure?
items.why: The medulla oblongata, part of the hindbrain, contains the vital centres that regulate heartbeat, respiration and blood pressure.

items.q: What is colostrum?
items.answer: Colostrum is the yellowish fluid secreted by the mammary glands during the first few days after childbirth, rich in antibodies (especially IgA) and nutrients, which provides passive immunity and nutrition to the newborn.

items.q: State one function of the cerebellum.
items.answer: The cerebellum maintains posture, balance and equilibrium of the body, and coordinates fine voluntary muscular movements and motor activities.

items.q: Name the causative agent and vector of malaria.
items.answer: Malaria is caused by the protozoan parasite Plasmodium and is transmitted by the bite of the female Anopheles mosquito, which acts as the vector.

items.q: What is artificial insemination?
items.answer: Artificial insemination is a technique in animal husbandry in which semen collected from a genetically superior male animal is artificially introduced into the reproductive tract of a female to achieve fertilization, improving the genetic quality of livestock.

items.q: What is a vector in genetic engineering? Give one example.
items.answer: A vector is a DNA molecule, such as a plasmid or bacteriophage, used as a vehicle to carry a foreign gene of interest into a host cell for its replication and expression. An example is the plasmid pBR322.

items.q: Define natality and mortality.
items.answer: Natality is the number of births occurring in a population per unit time, while mortality is the number of deaths occurring in a population per unit time; together with immigration and emigration, they determine population size.

items.q: What is the pyramid of energy? State its shape.
items.answer: The pyramid of energy represents the amount of energy present at each successive trophic level of an ecosystem. It is always upright in shape in every ecosystem, since the energy available progressively decreases at each higher trophic level due to the 10% law.

items.q: What is the Montreal Protocol?
items.answer: The Montreal Protocol is an international treaty signed in 1987 aimed at phasing out the production and use of ozone-depleting substances, particularly chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), to protect and restore the stratospheric ozone layer.

items.q: Describe the structure of a typical angiosperm ovule.
items.answer: A typical angiosperm ovule is attached to the placenta by a stalk called the funiculus, with the point of attachment of the body of the ovule to the funiculus called the hilum. The main body of the ovule is enclosed by one or two protective layers called integuments, which leave a small opening called the micropyle at the tip for pollen tube entry. Inside the integuments lies the nucellus, a mass of nutritive tissue, within which develops the haploid embryo sac (female gametophyte) containing the egg apparatus, polar nuclei and antipodal cells.

points.p: Funiculus, hilum and integuments with micropyle described
Nucellus and embryo sac within it correctly described

items.q: What is parturition? Name the hormone mainly responsible for inducing it.
items.answer: Parturition is the physiological process of childbirth, i.e. the expulsion of the fully developed fetus from the mother's uterus at the end of the gestation period, brought about by strong rhythmic uterine contractions. It is mainly induced by the hormone oxytocin, released from the posterior pituitary, which stimulates powerful contractions of the uterine (myometrial) muscles.

points.p: Correct definition of parturition
Correct hormone named (oxytocin) with its role

items.q: Define test cross. Explain its significance with an example.
items.answer: A test cross is a cross between an individual of unknown genotype (suspected heterozygous) and a homozygous recessive individual, used to determine the exact genotype of the unknown individual. For example, crossing a tall pea plant of unknown genotype with a homozygous dwarf plant (tt): if all offspring are tall, the unknown parent is homozygous dominant (TT); if offspring segregate in a 1:1 tall to dwarf ratio, the unknown parent is heterozygous (Tt).

points.p: Correct definition of test cross
Correct example showing how it reveals the unknown genotype

items.q: What is the genetic code? State one of its important features.
items.answer: The genetic code is the set of rules by which information encoded in the sequence of nucleotide triplets (codons) in mRNA is translated into the specific sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide during protein synthesis. One important feature is that the genetic code is degenerate, meaning that most amino acids are specified by more than one codon (e.g., leucine is coded by six different codons), which helps minimize the effect of mutations.

points.p: Correct definition of genetic code
Correct feature stated (e.g. degeneracy) with explanation

items.q: Define adaptive radiation with an example.
items.answer: Adaptive radiation is the evolutionary process by which a single ancestral species, upon migrating to a new geographically isolated region with diverse ecological niches, diversifies into multiple new species, each adapted to exploit a different niche or resource. A classic example is the Darwin's finches of the Galapagos Islands, which evolved from a common ancestral finch species into several species with differently shaped beaks adapted to different food sources (seeds, insects, nectar).

points.p: Correct definition of adaptive radiation
Correct example (e.g. Darwin's finches) explained

items.q: Explain guttation in plants.
items.answer: Guttation is the exudation of liquid water droplets (containing dissolved minerals and organic substances) from specialized pores called hydathodes, usually located at the leaf margins or tips of herbaceous plants. It occurs mainly at night or early morning when the soil is well watered, humidity is high, and transpiration is minimal, causing root pressure to build up and push excess xylem sap out through the hydathodes as liquid droplets rather than vapour.

points.p: Correct definition of guttation and hydathodes
Conditions favouring guttation (high root pressure, low transpiration, high humidity)

items.q: What is vernalization? Give one example of its practical application.
items.answer: Vernalization is the promotion of flowering in certain plants by prior exposure of the plant or its seeds to a period of low temperature, which is a prerequisite for them to flower normally in the subsequent growing season. A practical application is in winter wheat varieties, which are exposed to cold treatment before sowing so that they flower and produce grain within a single growing season instead of requiring an entire winter in the field.

points.p: Correct definition of vernalization
Correct practical application/example (e.g. winter wheat)

items.q: Define vital capacity and tidal volume in human respiration.
items.answer: Tidal volume is the volume of air inspired or expired during a single normal, quiet breath, approximately 500 mL in an adult human. Vital capacity is the maximum volume of air that can be forcibly expired after taking the deepest possible inspiration, representing the sum of inspiratory reserve volume, tidal volume and expiratory reserve volume, approximately 3500-4000 mL in a healthy adult.

points.p: Correct definition of tidal volume with approximate value
Correct definition of vital capacity with approximate value

items.q: Differentiate between the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous system.
items.answer: The sympathetic nervous system prepares the body for emergency 'fight or flight' responses, increasing heart rate, dilating pupils, diverting blood flow to skeletal muscles, and inhibiting digestive activity, using norepinephrine as its principal neurotransmitter at target organs. The parasympathetic nervous system promotes 'rest and digest' activities, slowing heart rate, constricting pupils, and stimulating digestive secretions and movements, using acetylcholine as its principal neurotransmitter at target organs; the two systems generally act antagonistically to maintain internal balance.

points.p: Correct description of sympathetic system functions and neurotransmitter
Correct description of parasympathetic system functions and neurotransmitter

items.q: What is an allergy? Name the chemical mediator mainly responsible for allergic symptoms.
items.answer: An allergy is a hypersensitivity reaction in which the immune system overreacts to normally harmless foreign substances called allergens (such as pollen, dust mites or certain foods), producing symptoms like sneezing, itching, watery eyes, or in severe cases anaphylaxis. The chemical mediator mainly responsible for these symptoms is histamine, which is released from mast cells upon exposure to the allergen and causes dilation of blood vessels and increased permeability.

points.p: Correct definition of allergy with example of allergens
Correct mediator named (histamine) with its role

items.q: What is Operation Flood? State its significance.
items.answer: Operation Flood was a dairy development programme launched in India in 1970 by the National Dairy Development Board, aimed at linking rural milk producers with urban consumers through a network of cooperative dairies, popularly associated with brands like Amul. Its significance lies in making India self-sufficient and eventually the largest milk producer in the world, while substantially improving the income and livelihood of millions of small rural dairy farmers.

points.p: Correct description of Operation Flood
Correct significance/outcome stated

items.q: What is PCR? State one of its applications.
items.answer: PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) is an in vitro technique used to amplify a specific segment of DNA into millions of copies within a few hours, using a thermostable DNA polymerase (Taq polymerase) and repeated cycles of denaturation, annealing and extension. One important application of PCR is in the early diagnosis of genetic and infectious diseases, as it can detect even minute amounts of a pathogen's or defective gene's DNA present in a patient sample.

points.p: Correct definition of PCR
Correct application stated (e.g. disease diagnosis/forensics)

items.q: Describe the process of pollination and its types with examples.
items.answer: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of a flower, which is essential for fertilization in flowering plants. Self-pollination (autogamy) is the transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma of the same flower, maintaining genetic purity, as seen in pea and wheat; geitonogamy is a type of self-pollination where pollen is transferred to another flower on the same plant. Cross-pollination (xenogamy) is the transfer of pollen from the anther of one flower to the stigma of a flower on a genetically different plant, producing greater genetic variation, and is carried out by various agents: anemophily (wind, e.g. grasses), hydrophily (water, e.g. Vallisneria), and entomophily/ornithophily (insects/birds, e.g. most flowering plants with colourful, scented flowers).

points.p: Correct definition of pollination and self-pollination with example
Correct definition of cross-pollination with example
Correct agents of pollination described (wind, water, insects/birds)

items.q: Describe the structure and events of oogenesis in humans.
items.answer: Oogenesis is the process of formation of the female gamete (ovum) in the ovary. It begins in the fetal stage, when oogonia undergo mitosis and differentiate into primary oocytes, which enter meiosis I but remain arrested at prophase (as primary oocytes within primary follicles) until puberty. At puberty, under hormonal stimulation, one primary oocyte completes meiosis I each month, dividing unequally to form a larger secondary oocyte and a small first polar body (which degenerates). The secondary oocyte begins meiosis II but again arrests at metaphase II, and is released at ovulation; it completes meiosis II, forming the mature ovum and a second polar body, only if it is penetrated by a sperm during fertilization.

points.p: Fetal origin of oogonia and formation of primary oocytes arrested at prophase I
Completion of meiosis I at puberty forming secondary oocyte and first polar body
Meiosis II arrest at metaphase II and completion only after fertilization

items.q: Explain the process of translation in brief.
items.answer: Translation is the process by which the sequence of codons on an mRNA molecule is decoded by ribosomes to synthesize a specific polypeptide chain. It begins with initiation, in which the small ribosomal subunit binds to the mRNA at the start codon (AUG), and the initiator tRNA carrying methionine binds to the ribosome, followed by attachment of the large ribosomal subunit to form a complete, functional ribosome. During elongation, charged tRNAs bring specific amino acids to the ribosome according to the codon sequence, and peptide bonds are formed sequentially between successive amino acids as the ribosome moves along the mRNA, lengthening the polypeptide chain. Finally, termination occurs when the ribosome reaches a stop codon (UAA, UAG or UGA), releasing the completed polypeptide chain and dissociating the ribosomal subunits from the mRNA.

points.p: Initiation: ribosome assembly at the start codon with initiator tRNA
Elongation: codon-by-codon addition of amino acids and peptide bond formation
Termination at the stop codon and release of the polypeptide

items.q: Describe two evidences supporting the theory of evolution.
items.answer: Fossil evidence: fossils are the preserved remains or impressions of organisms that lived in the past, found in sedimentary rock layers; the progressive increase in complexity of fossils from older (deeper) to younger (upper) rock strata provides a chronological record supporting gradual evolutionary change, as seen in the horse evolutionary series from Eohippus to modern Equus. Homologous organs: structures having the same basic structural plan and embryonic origin but modified to perform different functions in different organisms, such as the forelimbs of a frog, bird, horse, and human (all built on the same pentadactyl limb pattern but modified for walking, flying, running and grasping respectively), indicate that these organisms share a common evolutionary ancestor, a process called divergent evolution.

points.p: Fossil evidence correctly explained with example
Homologous organs correctly explained with example
Correct link of each evidence to the conclusion of common ancestry/gradual change

items.q: Explain the mechanism of stomatal opening and closing.
items.answer: Stomata are tiny pores on the leaf epidermis, each bounded by two kidney-shaped (or dumbbell-shaped in grasses) guard cells with unevenly thickened cell walls (thicker on the inner side facing the pore). According to the widely accepted potassium ion (K+) flux theory, in the presence of light, guard cells actively take up K+ ions (along with accompanying anions) from neighbouring cells, which decreases their water potential, causing water to enter the guard cells by osmosis; this increases the turgor pressure within the guard cells, and because the inner wall is thicker and less elastic than the outer wall, the cells bow outward, opening the pore. In darkness or under water stress, K+ ions move out of the guard cells (often under the influence of abscisic acid), water potential rises, water exits by osmosis, turgor pressure falls, and the guard cells straighten, closing the stomatal pore.

points.p: Correct structure of guard cells with uneven wall thickening described
Correct mechanism of opening: K+ influx, osmotic water entry, increased turgor bowing the guard cells outward
Correct mechanism of closing: K+ efflux, water loss, reduced turgor, pore closure

items.q: Explain the roles of cytokinins and abscisic acid as plant growth regulators.
items.answer: Cytokinins promote cell division (cytokinesis) in plant tissues, delay senescence (ageing) of leaves by maintaining protein and chlorophyll content, promote lateral bud growth by overcoming apical dominance, and are widely used in tissue culture media along with auxins to induce shoot formation from callus. Abscisic acid (ABA), often called the stress hormone, induces stomatal closure under water-deficit conditions by promoting efflux of potassium ions from guard cells, promotes seed dormancy and inhibits seed germination by counteracting the effects of gibberellins, and generally acts as a growth inhibitor, helping plants withstand unfavourable environmental conditions.

points.p: Correct functions of cytokinins (cell division, delay senescence, overcome apical dominance)
Correct functions of abscisic acid (stomatal closure, seed dormancy, growth inhibition)
Correct contrast between the growth-promoting and growth-inhibiting roles

items.q: Explain the transport of oxygen and carbon dioxide in human blood.
items.answer: Oxygen is transported mainly bound to haemoglobin in red blood cells, forming oxyhaemoglobin; each haemoglobin molecule can bind up to four oxygen molecules, and the extent of binding depends on the partial pressure of oxygen, with high pO2 in the alveoli favouring oxygen loading and lower pO2 in tissues favouring unloading. Carbon dioxide is transported in three forms: about 7% dissolved directly in blood plasma, about 20-23% bound to haemoglobin as carbaminohaemoglobin, and the majority, about 70%, is transported as bicarbonate ions (HCO3-) in plasma, formed when CO2 combines with water in red blood cells (catalyzed by the enzyme carbonic anhydrase) to form carbonic acid, which dissociates into H+ and HCO3-.

points.p: Correct oxygen transport mechanism via haemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin
Correct description of CO2 transport as dissolved and carbaminohaemoglobin forms
Correct description of the major bicarbonate transport pathway with carbonic anhydrase

items.q: Describe the structure and function of the human ear.
items.answer: The human ear consists of three regions. The outer ear includes the pinna, which collects sound waves, and the auditory canal, which directs them to the tympanic membrane (eardrum), causing it to vibrate. The middle ear is an air-filled cavity containing three small ear ossicles (malleus, incus and stapes), which mechanically amplify and transmit vibrations from the eardrum to the oval window of the inner ear, and is connected to the pharynx by the Eustachian tube, which equalizes air pressure. The inner ear contains the cochlea, a coiled, fluid-filled structure lined with hair cells that convert mechanical vibrations into nerve impulses (sent to the brain via the auditory nerve for the sensation of hearing), and the vestibular apparatus (semicircular canals, utricle and saccule), which detects changes in body position and balance.

points.p: Correct description of outer ear (pinna, auditory canal, eardrum)
Correct description of middle ear (ossicles, Eustachian tube)
Correct description of inner ear (cochlea for hearing, vestibular apparatus for balance)

items.q: Explain poultry farming and its scientific management practices.
items.answer: Poultry farming is the commercial rearing of domesticated birds, mainly chickens, for the production of eggs (layer birds) and meat (broiler birds). Scientific management includes selective breeding and cross-breeding of indigenous breeds (disease-resistant) with exotic breeds (high-yielding) to develop improved varieties suited to local conditions, along with maintaining hygienic, well-ventilated housing with controlled temperature and adequate space to minimize stress and disease spread. Proper nutrition through balanced, protein-rich feed, regular vaccination schedules against diseases such as Ranikhet disease and fowl pox, and clean water supply are essential, and such scientific management has made India one of the leading global producers of eggs and poultry meat, improving rural nutrition and livelihoods.

points.p: Correct definition of poultry farming (layers and broilers)
Breeding and housing management correctly described
Nutrition, vaccination and overall significance correctly described

items.q: Explain the exponential and logistic models of population growth.
items.answer: The exponential (J-shaped) growth model applies when resources (food, space) are unlimited, described by the equation dN/dt = rN, where N is population size, r is the intrinsic rate of natural increase, and t is time; growth accelerates continuously without any check, producing a J-shaped curve when plotted against time. The logistic (S-shaped/sigmoid) growth model is more realistic, applying when resources are limited, described by dN/dt = rN(K-N)/K, where K is the carrying capacity of the environment; growth is initially exponential but progressively slows as the population size (N) approaches K due to increasing intraspecific competition, eventually stabilizing at K. Most natural populations follow the logistic model because resources are finite in real environments.

points.p: Correct exponential growth equation and description of the J-shaped curve
Correct logistic growth equation and description of the S-shaped curve
Correct explanation of why most natural populations follow the logistic model (finite resources, carrying capacity)

items.q: Explain ecological succession, describing its main types.
items.answer: Ecological succession is the natural, gradual and sequential change in the species composition of a biological community over time, ultimately leading to the development of a relatively stable climax community adapted to the prevailing environmental conditions. Primary succession occurs on newly exposed substrates that have never previously supported life, such as bare rock, sand dunes, or newly cooled lava, beginning with pioneer species like lichens and mosses; it is a very slow process taking hundreds to thousands of years. Secondary succession occurs on sites that previously supported life but were disturbed or destroyed by events such as fire, flood, or deforestation, and proceeds much faster than primary succession since soil and some organisms already exist; succession in water bodies progressing toward land is called hydrarch succession, while succession in dry regions progressing toward moister conditions is called xerarch succession.

points.p: Correct definition of ecological succession and climax community
Correct description of primary succession with example
Correct description of secondary succession, and hydrarch/xerarch types

items.q: Explain the concept and levels of biodiversity.
items.answer: Biodiversity refers to the variety and variability of life forms found on earth, and is studied at three hierarchical levels. Genetic diversity is the variation in genes and alleles within a single species, giving rise to variation among individuals and populations, such as the many rice varieties differing in yield and disease resistance. Species diversity is the variety and abundance of different species present within a particular region or ecosystem, often assessed in terms of species richness (number of species) and species evenness (relative abundance of each). Ecological (ecosystem) diversity is the variety of distinct ecosystem types, such as deserts, forests, wetlands and coral reefs, found within a geographical region, each with its own unique community structure and function; all three levels together determine the overall health and resilience of the biosphere.

points.p: Correct definition of genetic diversity with example
Correct definition of species diversity (richness and evenness)
Correct definition of ecological diversity with examples

items.q: Describe the structure of the mature embryo sac of an angiosperm with a labeled diagram, and explain the role of each component.
items.answer: The mature (7-celled, 8-nucleate) embryo sac is the female gametophyte formed inside the nucellus of the ovule after meiosis of the megaspore mother cell and three mitotic divisions of the functional megaspore. At the micropylar end lies the egg apparatus, consisting of one egg cell (which fuses with a male gamete during syngamy to form the zygote) flanked by two synergid cells, which secrete chemotropic substances that guide the entry of the pollen tube into the embryo sac and help in the discharge of male gametes (the synergids show a special filiform apparatus for this purpose). At the opposite, chalazal end lie three antipodal cells, which are nutritive in function and eventually degenerate. In the centre of the embryo sac is a large central cell containing two polar nuclei, which fuse with the second male gamete during triple fusion to form the triploid primary endosperm nucleus, which later develops into the nutritive endosperm. Diagram: draw an oval embryo sac showing the egg apparatus (egg cell with two synergids) at the micropylar end, three antipodal cells at the chalazal end, and the large central cell with two polar nuclei in the middle, all correctly labeled.

points.p: Correct description of egg apparatus (egg cell and two synergids) with synergid function
Correct description of antipodal cells and their nutritive, degenerating role
Correct description of central cell with two polar nuclei and their role in triple fusion
Correctly labeled diagram of the 7-celled, 8-nucleate embryo sac

items.q: (a) Explain the sex-linked inheritance pattern of red-green colour blindness in humans. (b) Draw/describe a pedigree chart for a colour-blind son born to a phenotypically normal father and a carrier (heterozygous) mother.
items.answer: (a) The gene for red-green colour blindness is located on the X chromosome and is recessive; since males have only one X chromosome (XY), a single recessive allele (Xc) on their X chromosome is sufficient to make them colour-blind, whereas females (XX) need the recessive allele on both X chromosomes to be colour-blind, and are carriers (phenotypically normal but can pass the allele to offspring) if they carry it on only one X chromosome. This explains why colour blindness is far more common in males than in females, and why an affected father cannot pass the trait to his sons (who receive his Y chromosome), but can pass the carrier allele to his daughters. (b) In the given family, the father (XY, normal) contributes either X or Y to offspring, while the carrier mother (XcX, phenotypically normal) contributes either Xc or X. A son receiving Xc from the mother and Y from the father becomes colour-blind (XcY); a son receiving X from the mother and Y from the father is normal (XY); a daughter receiving Xc from the mother and X from the father becomes a carrier (XcX, normal phenotype); a daughter receiving X from both parents is normal (XX). Diagram: draw a pedigree with the father (filled-border square, normal) and mother (half-filled circle, carrier) at the top, connected to four possible offspring symbols below - unfilled square (normal son), filled square (affected son), half-filled circle (carrier daughter), and unfilled circle (normal daughter) - with standard pedigree symbols and a key.

points.p: Correct explanation of X-linked recessive inheritance and why males are more often affected
Correct explanation of carrier female concept
Correct genotype/phenotype combinations of all four possible offspring
Correctly described/drawn pedigree chart with standard symbols and key

items.q: Describe the mechanism of inspiration and expiration in humans, and explain the role of the diaphragm and intercostal muscles with reference to lung volumes.
items.answer: Breathing involves two phases driven by changes in thoracic volume and pressure. During inspiration, the diaphragm contracts and flattens (moving downward), while the external intercostal muscles contract, lifting the ribcage upward and outward; together these increase the volume of the thoracic cavity, which lowers the intrapulmonary (intra-alveolar) pressure below atmospheric pressure, causing air to flow passively into the lungs down the pressure gradient. During expiration, the diaphragm relaxes and resumes its dome shape (moving upward), while the external intercostal muscles relax and the internal intercostal muscles may contract, decreasing thoracic volume, which raises intrapulmonary pressure above atmospheric pressure and forces air out of the lungs. Both normal inspiration and expiration are largely driven by these pressure gradient changes; during forceful breathing, additional accessory muscles (e.g. abdominal muscles during forced expiration) are recruated. The resulting lung volumes include tidal volume (~500 mL, air moved in one normal breath), inspiratory reserve volume (~2500-3000 mL, extra air that can be forcibly inhaled after a normal inspiration), expiratory reserve volume (~1000-1100 mL, extra air that can be forcibly exhaled after a normal expiration), and residual volume (~1100-1200 mL, air that always remains in the lungs even after maximum forced expiration, preventing lung collapse).

points.p: Correct mechanism of inspiration: diaphragm and external intercostal contraction increasing thoracic volume, lowering pressure
Correct mechanism of expiration: diaphragm and intercostal relaxation decreasing thoracic volume, raising pressure
Correct explanation that air movement follows the pressure gradient created by volume change
Correct description of at least two lung volumes (tidal volume, residual volume, etc.) with approximate values

items.q: Describe the structure of the human brain (forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain) with a labeled diagram, explaining the function of each major region.
items.answer: The human brain has three major divisions. The forebrain includes the cerebrum, the largest and most developed part, divided into two cerebral hemispheres connected by the corpus callosum, which controls voluntary movements, sensory perception, memory, learning, reasoning and intelligence; the thalamus, which relays sensory information to the cerebral cortex; and the hypothalamus, which regulates body temperature, hunger, thirst, and controls the pituitary gland, linking the nervous and endocrine systems. The midbrain is a small region connecting the forebrain and hindbrain, containing centres involved in visual and auditory reflexes (such as pupillary reflex) and controlling certain eye movements. The hindbrain consists of the cerebellum, which maintains posture, balance and coordinates fine voluntary muscular movements; the pons, which relays signals between different parts of the brain and is involved in regulating respiration; and the medulla oblongata, which controls vital involuntary functions such as heartbeat, breathing rate, blood pressure and reflexes like coughing, sneezing and vomiting. Diagram: draw a sagittal section of the human brain showing the cerebrum, thalamus, hypothalamus, midbrain, cerebellum, pons and medulla oblongata, each correctly labeled in their relative positions.

points.p: Correct description of forebrain (cerebrum, thalamus, hypothalamus) and their functions
Correct description of midbrain and its reflex functions
Correct description of hindbrain (cerebellum, pons, medulla) and their functions
Correctly labeled diagram of the brain showing all major regions

items.q: What is gene therapy? Explain with reference to the treatment of ADA deficiency, and briefly explain how human insulin is produced using recombinant DNA technology.
items.answer: Gene therapy is a biotechnological approach to treating a genetic disorder by correcting the underlying defective gene, either by inserting a normal functional copy of the gene into the patient's cells to compensate for the non-functional one, or by replacing/repairing the defective gene directly. The first clinical application of gene therapy was for Adenosine Deaminase (ADA) deficiency, a severe combined immunodeficiency disorder caused by a defect in the gene coding for the ADA enzyme, essential for proper functioning of lymphocytes. In this procedure, lymphocytes are extracted from the patient's blood, grown in culture outside the body, and a functional ADA gene is introduced into these cells using a retroviral vector; these genetically corrected lymphocytes are then reintroduced into the patient's body, where they begin producing the missing ADA enzyme. Since these genetically modified lymphocytes are not permanently self-renewing, the patient may need periodic infusions of such engineered cells, though a more permanent cure could involve introducing the normal gene into early embryonic stem cells. Human insulin production using recombinant DNA technology involves inserting the genes coding for the A and B polypeptide chains of human insulin separately into plasmid vectors, which are then introduced into Escherichia coli bacteria; the bacteria express and produce the two insulin chains separately, which are subsequently extracted, purified and combined by forming disulfide bonds to produce complete, biologically active human insulin, marketed as Humulin, avoiding the allergic reactions sometimes caused by earlier animal-derived insulin.

points.p: Correct definition of gene therapy
Correct explanation of the ADA deficiency gene therapy procedure (extraction, retroviral vector insertion, reintroduction)
Correct explanation that periodic treatment/more permanent stem-cell approach may be needed
Correct explanation of recombinant human insulin production in E. coli (A and B chains, combination via disulfide bonds)
